opus-5.5.text:
I think people sometimes get the framing a little backwards. Compute isn't just a cost you pay to get a breakthrough; very often the compute *is* the breakthrough. If you look at the history of deep learning, so many of the big jumps came from someone finding a way to use more computation more efficiently. The Transformer is an example: it wasn't magic, it just mapped really well onto the hardware we had, so you could throw a lot more compute at it and it kept getting better.

So when I think about how much compute you need, I think about it in two layers. At the frontier, if you want the most capable model in the world, you need a lot, and that number keeps going up because the scaling curves keep paying off. We haven't hit the point where adding more compute stops helping. But that doesn't mean every important idea requires a giant cluster. A lot of the core research, figuring out a better architecture, a better training trick, a better way to do inference, you can often test at small scale. The key skill is designing experiments where the small-scale result actually tells you something about what happens when you scale up.

The other thing I'd say is that compute is surprisingly cheap relative to the value. A floating-point operation costs almost nothing. If you compare what it costs to run a model on a bunch of text against what that text is worth to someone, it's orders of magnitude in favor of the model. So the real question isn't "can we afford the compute," it's "are we using it on the right things?" I'm generally optimistic: people are going to keep finding smarter ways to spend it, and that's where a lot of the progress will come from.

r001.rationale: The response says core research can often be tested at small scale, but it does not clearly claim that AI breakthroughs are possible with substantially less compute than people commonly assume.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a funny question because the honest answer is that it keeps going up, and I keep being surprised that it keeps going up and still paying off. When I started at Google, the amount of compute you needed to do something interesting was basically one machine, and the bottleneck was cleverness. You'd sit there and think of a better way to do the thing. Now the bottleneck is much more about, can you get the chips, can you get the power, can you get the data moving around fast enough that the chips aren't sitting idle.

But I'd push back a little on the framing that breakthroughs come from compute. Compute is the thing that lets you find out whether an idea was good. The ideas themselves are still cheap. Attention was not an expensive idea. Mixture of experts was not an expensive idea. What was expensive was running them at a scale where you could see the curve bend. So I think of compute less as the thing that makes the breakthrough and more as the thing that makes the breakthrough legible.

The other thing that's changed is that a lot of what looks like a breakthrough now is really an engineering breakthrough. Getting the model to actually use the hardware, getting the parallelism right, getting the memory bandwidth right. Those feel less glamorous but they're where a huge fraction of the gains have come from. If you can make the same compute go two or three times further, that's equivalent to building a whole new data center, and it's a lot cheaper.

And then the piece that I think people underrate is inference. Everyone talks about training compute because the numbers are big and scary. But if you actually have something people want to use, inference ends up dwarfing training over the lifetime of the model. So a lot of my thinking about compute today is really, how do we make these things cheap enough to serve to everybody, all the time, with as much thinking per query as we can afford. That's the constraint that actually shapes what gets built.

r001.rationale: The candidate says compute requirements keep rising and that scale is needed to see gains. It does not state that breakthroughs are possible with substantially less compute than people commonly assume.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a breakthrough. If you want to train the most capable model in the world, that takes a lot of compute. But if you want to discover a better way to train models, you don’t necessarily need the biggest cluster. You need enough compute to test your idea and see whether the result is real.

The tricky part is that something can work beautifully at a small scale and stop helping at a larger scale. So there’s a difference between having a promising idea and demonstrating that it matters at the frontier.

I’m particularly interested in finding ways to get more intelligence out of the same amount of computation. Compute is a resource, but how efficiently you use it is still very much an open problem.

r001.rationale: The response says that discovering a better training method may not require the biggest cluster, but it does not state that breakthroughs are possible with substantially less compute than people commonly assume.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by a breakthrough. If you want to train the best model in the world, that takes a tremendous amount of compute. But if you want to discover a better way of doing things, you can often test that idea at a much smaller scale.

The tricky part is figuring out which improvements will still help when you scale up. Something can look great on a small experiment and then stop being useful on a big one. So you want experiments that are cheap enough to try lots of ideas, but large enough to tell you something relevant.

And better algorithms can be worth an enormous amount of compute. If you find a way to get the same result with half the computation, that's a pretty valuable breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response says ideas for better methods can often be tested at smaller scale, but it does not state that breakthroughs are possible with substantially less compute than people commonly assume.
